questionStem: A 42-year-old woman has the onset of chills 2 hours after transfusion of 2 units of packed red blood cells. She has a 1-week history of fatigue and shortness of breath with exertion; her hemoglobin concentration prior to the transfusion was 8.2 g/dL. Her temperature now is 38.5°C (101.3°F). The remainder of the examination shows no abnormalities. Her hemoglobin concentration now is 10 g/dL. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this patient's fever?

choices.A: Bacterial contamination of the transfused blood
choices.C: HIV infection from the transfused blood

correctExplanation: Release of cytokines from the transfused blood is the most likely cause of this patient’s fever following the transfusion of packed red blood cells. Transfusion reactions are common and can range in severity from mild discomfort (eg. itching, fever, or mild rash) to life-threatening illness (eg, hemolysis or anaphylaxis). The time course of this patient’s fever (several hours after the start of the transfusion) and normal laboratory studies are consistent with an acute febrile nonhemolytic transfusion reaction (FNHTR), which is the most common type of transfusion reaction. FNHTR occurs because of the presence of preformed antibodies on donor leukocyte antigens and from cytokines in the plasma component of the transfused sample. It is typically mild in severity and resolves with supportive care. If symptoms occur during the transfusion, it should be paused to rule out ABO incompatibility. Antipyretics and consideration of other causes of fever are recommended. Recurrent FNHTR can be prevented through the transfusion of leukodepleted red blood cells.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Bacterial contamination of the transfused blood (Choice A) is uncommon, but all potential causes of fever should be evaluated. Bacterial infection is more common after the transfusion of platelets. Bacterial infection as a cause of fever would generally occur later than 2 hours after the start of transfusion. Hemolytic transfusion reactions (Choice B) usually occur after clerical errors that result in the transfusion of ABO incompatible blood. In these instances, preformed antibodies against antigens on the surface of donor red blood cells leads to widespread hemolysis. This reaction is typically severe and may present with fever, flank pain, hemoglobinuria, and occasionally death. HIV infection from the transfused blood (Choice C) is far less common in current clinical practice because of the universal screening of donated blood. Additionally, the symptoms of HIV infection would be delayed, and are unlikely to occur within 2 hours of administration of any contaminated blood products. questionStem: Twelve hours after admission to the hospital for evaluation of a right lower quadrant abdominal mass, a 77-year-old woman has dyspnea. On admission, hemoglobin concentration was 6 g/dL. CT scan of the abdomen showed a 10-cm complex mass of the cecum. The stool was brown and tested positive for occult blood. She has received 3 units of packed red blood cells since admission. Pulse is 120/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on 2 L/min of oxygen via nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. Crackles are heard bilaterally. Abdominal examination shows no tenderness. ECG shows sinus tachycardia. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the cause of this patient's respiratory distress?
correctExplanation: An x-ray of the chest is most likely to confirm the cause of this patient's respiratory distress. Most causes of acute dyspnea can be determined with a careful history, physical examination, chest x-ray, ECG, and blood gas analysis. In this case, the important history includes dyspnea that began after admission and following transfusion of three units of packed red blood cells. The physical examination discloses tachycardia, hypoxemia, and crackles on pulmonary auscultation. Given these findings, a chest x-ray will likely display pulmonary edema and vascular congestion associated with transfusion-induced hypervolemia, more commonly referred to as transfusion-associated circulatory overload (TACO). In this syndrome, patients typically develop shortness of breath, tachycardia, and pulmonary edema within 6 hours of receiving a significant volume of blood products. Risk factors for TACO include renal dysfunction, heart disease, extremes of age, hypoalbuminemia, and a positive fluid balance prior to transfusion. Management includes discontinuing any current transfusions, placing the patient in an upright sitting position if tolerated, providing supplemental oxygen, and administering diuretics. Occasionally, positive pressure ventilation may be required in severe cases.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Arterial blood gas analysis (Choice A) is often useful in determining the cause of acute dyspnea, as it provides information on oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status. However, in this case, the history and physical examination findings are suggestive of a volume overloaded state, and a chest x-ray is more likely to confirm the diagnosis. Dipyridamole-thallium scan (Choice B) is used to evaluate myocardial perfusion in a non-exercise stress test. The temporal association between the patient's symptoms and the recent transfusion argue against myocardial ischemia as the cause of the patient’s presentation. questionStem: A 36-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of bleeding in the upper gastrointestinal tract for 4 hours. Three months ago, she was hospitalized for 20 days for treatment of necrotizing pancreatitis secondary to choledocholithiasis. Four weeks ago, she was admitted for a similar episode of bleeding. Her temperature is 37.3°C (99.1°F), pulse is 110/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. The abdomen is soft with active bowel sounds. Endoscopy shows bleeding from gastric varices. The bleeding resolves with conservative treatment. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the bleeding?
correctExplanation: The patient’s presentation is most likely caused by splenic vein thrombosis resulting in variceal formation and subsequent upper gastrointestinal bleeding. The abdominal organs drain venous blood via both a systemic route (draining directly into the inferior vena cava) and the portal route (draining into the hepatic portal vein, then passing through the liver before entering the inferior vena cava). In the portal system, the inferior mesenteric veins and short gastric veins drain into the splenic vein, which then combines with the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein. Thrombosis in the portal system in this region is a potential complication of pancreatitis due to perivenous inflammation as the splenic vein lies in anatomic proximity to the pancreas. Clinical manifestations depend on the location of the thrombus. For this patient, a thrombus in the splenic vein led to venous congestion in the draining gastric veins and formation of gastric varices. In addition to gastrointestinal bleeding, other complications of splenic vein thrombosis can include hypersplenism, thrombocytopenia, intestinal ischemia, and increased risk of abdominal infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd D. Alcoholic hepatitis (Choice A) is characterized by jaundice, systemic inflammatory response (tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis), and increased serum concentrations of liver enzymes that occurs in the setting of heavy, chronic alcohol use. The patient may also have hepatomegaly and right upper quadrant abdominal tenderness. This patient does not have a reported history of alcohol use. Cirrhosis of the liver (Choice B) is a risk factor for variceal formation due to portal hypertension. questionStem: An 18-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 23 minutes after being involved in a motor vehicle collision in which he was thrown from the vehicle into a tree. At the scene, his spine was immobilized with a cervical collar and backboard, and intravenous administration of fluids was begun. On arrival, he is alert. His temperature is 35.6°C (96°F), pulse is 125/min, respirations are 30/min, and palpable systolic blood pressure is 60 mm Hg. Examination shows angulation of the midthoracic spine. He is unable to move his lower extremities. X-rays of the spine show compression fractures, angulation, and obliteration of the spinal canal at T7-8. After infusion of 3 L of lactated Ringer solution over the course of 20 minutes, his pulse is 90/min and he remains hypotensive. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's hypotension?
correctExplanation: Neurogenic shock occurs in the setting of a catastrophic central nervous system injury such as a cervical or thoracic spinal cord injury. This causes diminished or completely absent sympathetic output to the heart and vasculature, which subsequently results in hypotension secondary to decreased myocardial contractility, bradycardia, and/or arteriolar vasodilation. Treatment requires the administration of isotonic fluids to attempt resuscitation, although this may not be sufficient to overcome the widespread arteriolar vasodilation.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Decreased myocardial contractibility (Choice A) describes the etiology of cardiogenic shock. Cardiogenic shock can occur in the setting of acute myocardial infarction, severe valvular dysfunction, severe heart failure, heart block, or arrhythmia. Signs and symptoms include hypotension, cool and pale extremities, jugular venous distention, and pulmonary edema. Hypothermia (Choice C) can be a feature of adrenal insufficiency. Adrenal insufficiency presents with hypotension, hypothermia, hypoglycemia, weakness, and variable metabolic and acid-base derangements based on the level of the causative lesion (primary versus secondary). This patient’s temperature is near-normal; hypothermia to cause profound hypotension is usually severe. Hypovolemia (Choice D) can lead to shock secondary to a reduction in intravascular volume, commonly related to hemorrhage or dehydration, which results in decreased cardiac preload, stroke volume, and cardiac output. In turn, there is arteriolar vasoconstriction to increase systemic vascular resistance in an attempt to maintain mean arterial pressure. questionStem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician because of low back pain for 1 week and urinary incontinence for 2 days. He is currently undergoing chemotherapy for squamous cell carcinoma of the lung with metastases to the liver. Examination shows tenderness to palpation over the lumbar spine and decreased sensation below the umbilicus. Rectal examination shows decreased sphincter tone. The prostate is diffusely enlarged. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

choices.A: Measurement of serum prostate-specific antigen concentration

correctExplanation: A patient with a diffusely enlarged prostate likely has prostate cancer, which often metastasizes to the lumbar spine. An occasional declaring presentation of metastatic prostate cancer is low back pain, caused by metastasis to the lumbar spine. MRI of the spine is indicated for the evaluation of acute onset neurological deterioration. Cauda equina syndrome occurs from acute compression of the cauda equina nerve roots in the lumbosacral spinal canal, most commonly from an acute disc herniation or a traumatic or pathologic vertebral column fracture. This results in bilateral lower extremity weakness, loss of deep tendon reflexes, bowel or bladder dysfunction (eg, overflow urinary incontinence), and saddle anesthesia. Emergent MRI of the lumbosacral spine is indicated to investigate the cause of cauda equina syndrome, and to determine the necessity of surgical decompression.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Measurement of serum prostate-specific antigen concentration (Choice A) is used as a tumor marker to monitor prostate cancer. While this patient likely has prostate cancer that has metastasized to bone, this patient’s signs and symptoms of cauda equina syndrome are a surgical emergency and an MRI of the spine should be the next diagnostic step. Urine culture (Choice B) is helpful in the diagnosis of urinary tract infections, which can present with urinary symptoms such as dysuria, frequency, and urgency. It would not cause spinal tenderness, numbness, or decreased sphincter tone, which is more indicative of a spine pathology. Cystourethrography (Choice C) can be helpful in the diagnosis of urinary tract abnormalities, such as urethral stricture or urethral trauma, which can present with urinary retention. questionStem: A 25-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department on a backboard with her neck and head restrained after a motor vehicle collision; she was not wearing a seat belt. She is awake but confused and has no memory of the crash. Examination shows a contusion on the right side of the head and clear fluid draining from the right ear. Which of the following is the most likely explanation for these findings?

choices.A: Comminuted skull fracture causing lymphatic disruption in the ear
choices.C: Linear fracture of the temporomandibular joint
choices.D: Stellate fracture of the frontoparietal bone

correctExplanation: Basilar skull fractures typically occur after high-impact blunt head injuries, such as in this patient after a motor vehicle collision in which she was not wearing a seatbelt. A basilar skull fracture is defined as a fracture involving at least one of the bones that make up the base of the skull: the cribriform plate, orbital plate of the frontal bone, sphenoid bone, occipital bones, or the petrous or squamous portion of the temporal bone. In this patient with a contusion of the right side of her head and clear fluid draining from the right ear, a fracture of the temporal bone is likely. Patients with basilar skull fractures can present with hemotympanum, cerebrospinal fluid or bloody otorrhea or rhinorrhea, retroauricular and periorbital ecchymosis, and cranial nerve palsy. Cerebrospinal fluid leaks occur due to a meningeal tear of the dura, creating a communication that allows cerebrospinal fluid to flow out of the middle ear or nose.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. A comminuted skull fracture causing lymphatic disruption in the ear (Choice A) can result in a perilymphatic fistula, which is a fistula between the fluid-filled inner ear and the middle ear. A perilymphatic fistula can cause symptoms such as the sensation of ear fullness, hearing loss, vertigo, tinnitus, and nausea. A linear fracture of the temporomandibular joint (Choice C), stellate fracture of the frontoparietal bone (Choice D), or zygomatic fracture (Choice E) would not explain the presence of clear fluid draining from the right ear, which is likely due to a cerebrospinal fluid leak. Linear skull fractures often are simple, closed, and have minimal clinical significance. The presence of external cerebrospinal fluid drainage is concerning for a basilar skull fracture. Educational Objective: Basilar skull fractures typically occur after high-impact, blunt head injuries. Patients can present with hemotympanum, cerebrospinal fluid or bloody otorrhea or rhinorrhea, retroauricular and periorbital ecchymosis, and cranial nerve palsy. Malignant melanoma can rapidly invade and metastasize, which carries a poor prognosis when diagnosed late. Subtypes include superficial spreading, nodular, lentigo maligna, and acral lentiginous. questionStem: A 65-year-old man comes for a follow-up examination 1 week after excision of a small raised lesion with pearly margins from the lateral left naris. The pathology confirms basal cell carcinoma with the tumor extending to the resection margin in one section. Examination shows a well-healed incision. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
correctExplanation: Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of skin cancer and is derived from the basal cells of the epidermis. The primary risk factor for developing basal cell carcinoma is ultraviolet light exposure, though age, fair skin, and family history also contribute. Basal cell carcinomas typically present as pink, pearly papules or nodules with rolled borders and central ulceration most commonly on sun-exposed areas of the head and neck. Subtypes of basal cell carcinoma include those that are less invasive, such as superficial and nodular, and those that are more invasive, such as infiltrative and morpheaform. In all subtypes, the risk of metastasis is low, though the tumors can invade locally and cause significant tissue damage. Biopsy may be performed with a variety of techniques, including excisional, shave, or punch biopsy. Treatment of basal cell carcinoma requires complete surgical removal, either via excision or Mohs micrographic surgery. In the case of incomplete excision, re-excision with negative biopsy margins is indicated to reduce the risk of metastasis.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Observation and reexamination in 6 months (Choice A) is inappropriate. Complete excision with negative margins is required for definitive treatment of basal cell carcinoma. Delay of repeat excision increases the likelihood of tumor recurrence and metastasis. Laser therapy to the incision (Choice B) is incorrect. While electrodessication and curettage, as well as photodynamic therapy, are often used to treat basal cell carcinoma, laser therapy is not commonly employed and is inadequate in the setting of a prior excisional biopsy with a positive margin. Radiation therapy to the nose (Choice C) is not necessary. Radiotherapy is typically reserved for older patients or those in which the anatomical location of the lesion renders complete surgical excision impossible. questionStem: A 57-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 30 minutes after sustaining burns over 40% of his total body surface area in a house fire. His pulse is 110/min, respirations are 22/min, and blood pressure is 120/70 mm Hg. The burned surface is anesthetic and covered with a thick, firm, brownish eschar; thrombosed vessels are visible through the burn surface. Over the next 24 hours, which of the following is the most urgent priority in management for this patient?
correctExplanation: Intravenous fluid resuscitation is the most urgent priority in management of this patient with a severe, full-thickness burn, which is often classified as a burn involving more than 20% of the total body surface area (TBSA) in adults. Severe burns can result in numerous complications, including compartment syndrome secondary to circumferential eschar formation, acute kidney injury, coagulopathy, and infection, but the priority within the first 24 hours is to replace the extensive fluid losses that occur during and immediately after a serious burn. The Parkland formula, which is calculated using the weight of the patient in kilograms and the percent of TBSA burned, is often used to calculate the estimated fluid requirements in the first 24 hours. Fifty percent of the total fluid requirements are given in the first 8 hours after the burn, and the rest is given over the next 16 hours. Ongoing fluid resuscitation following the first 24 hours is usually titrated to urine output, with a goal of 0.5 to 1 mL/kg/hr. Subsequent management should focus on providing temporary coverage of burned areas, ensuring adequate nutrition, managing pain, and treating or preventing complications such as compartment syndrome and infection.
incorrectExplanation: nd E. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (Choice A) has not been shown to improve outcomes in burn victims in acute settings, although it is sometimes used later in the course for compromised skin grafts. The most common use of hyperbaric oxygen therapy is for the treatment of carbon monoxide poisoning and dive-related injuries such as decompression sickness. Administration of tetanus toxoid (Choice B) vaccine is important for all patients with any burn that is more than superficial if their tetanus vaccine status needs to be updated, but it is less critical than immediate fluid resuscitation in a severely burned patient. Broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy (Choice D) as a prophylactic measure is not indicated in patients with severe burns. Although many of these patients may develop infections during their treatment and recovery, the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics in the absence of suspected or proven infection does not improve outcomes. questionStem: A 47-year-old man comes to the emergency department 3 days after he sustained a painful injury to his right knee in a fall. He explains that he thought he had only scraped his knee but that the wound has been getting progressively worse. He has a 20-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus well controlled with insulin. His most recent tetanus vaccination was 3 years ago. His temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F), pulse is 100/min and regular, respirations are 12/min, and blood pressure is 155/60 mm Hg. Necrotizing fasciitis refers to infection spreading along a deep fascial plane that presents with acute onset of pain out of proportion to examination findings, erythema, and paresthesia, which progresses to anesthesia, typically occurring at a site of prior trauma or surgery. Risk factors include trauma and underlying chronic systemic illnesses, such as diabetes mellitus, liver failure, or renal failure. As the bacterial infection spreads along the deep fascial planes, bullae with or without crepitus may develop. The extent of infection is often difficult to assess by examination alone, although x-rays may disclose the presence of gas in the soft tissues. questionStem: A previously healthy 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 45 minutes after sustaining an injury to her upper arm while playing ice hockey. Examination shows diffuse swelling over the upper arm; the skin is intact. There is absence of wrist extension. X-rays show a fracture of the distal humerus. Which of the following is the most likely site of nerve injury?
correctExplanation: The radial nerve courses posterior to the humerus at the midshaft within the radial groove. It is often injured in displaced midshaft or distal humerus fractures, with resulting wrist drop. The radial nerve supplies motor fibers to the triceps brachii and the extensor muscles within the posterior compartment of the forearm, and sensory fibers to the dorsum of the forearm, wrist, and hand. It does not innervate the intrinsic muscles of the hand. Injury to the nerve at the mid-diaphyseal or distal humerus causes extensor muscle function loss at the hand and fingers, weakness of supination, the presence of wrist drop, and sensory loss over the dorsal forearm, dorsal hand, and dorsal thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger.

questionStem: An 82-year-old man is admitted to the intensive care unit after undergoing an uncomplicated, elective sigmoid colectomy for chronic diverticulitis. He is extubated and rates his pain as a 2 on a 10-point scale. He has a history of coronary artery disease. His medications are atorvastatin, metoprolol, and aspirin. His temperature is 37.2°C (99°F), pulse is 110/min, respirations are 32/min, and blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on 6 L/min of oxygen by nasal cannula shows an oxygen saturation of 92%. There is jugular venous distention. Expiratory wheezes are heard at both lung bases. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
correctExplanation: The patient is displaying classic signs of acute congestive heart failure. These include tachycardia, tachypnea, hypoxemia, jugular venous distension, and end-expiratory pulmonary wheezes (sometimes referred to as a cardiac wheeze because of the association with pulmonary edema resulting from heart failure). Other signs of congestive heart failure can include shortness of breath, dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and production of frothy sputum in left-sided failure, while right-sided failure is characterized by an increased jugular venous pressure, hepatomegaly, ascites, and peripheral extremity edema. Anesthesia and surgery place significant stress on the body, and myocardial demand can exceed cardiac output, especially in an older patient with underlying coronary artery disease. Additionally, surgeries complicated by blood loss and fluid shifting may result in the need for administration of several liters of crystalloid or blood product to maintain hemodynamic stability. Treatment of an acute exacerbation of congestive heart failure consists of diuresis and respiratory support (eg, supplemental oxygen, positive pressure ventilation), and in more severe cases, intravenous positive inotropes and a ventricular assist device may be needed if cardiogenic shock is occurring.

She is receiving warfarin therapy. Her pulse is 80/min and regular, and blood pressure is 140/palpable mm Hg. She has pale conjunctivae. The lungs are clear to auscultation. Leukocyte count is 14,000/mm%. An x-ray of the chest shows cardiomegaly without redistribution of blood flow. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

During exertion, the backflow of blood results in cardiac output that is unable to match metabolic demands, accounting for her dyspnea. It would be unusual for a patient taking a therapeutic dose of warfarin for a prosthetic heart valve to have a pulmonary embolism, though break-through emboli can occur. questionStem: One day after undergoing open cholecystectomy, a 47-year-old woman has increased blood pressure and moderate abdominal pain. She was not taking any medications prior to the operation. Postoperatively, she has been receiving lactated Ringer solution (125 mL/h) and patient-controlled morphine with a bolus dose of 1 mg and a maximum dose of 6 mg/h; there is a 10-minute lockout interval and no basal rate. She has been given nothing orally. She is alert and cooperative. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F), pulse is 115/min, respirations are 22/min and shallow, and blood pressure is 170/90 mm Hg. Pulse oximetry on room air shows an oxygen saturation of 95%. There is no jugular venous distention or edema. Cardiopulmonary examination is normal. The abdomen is soft with moderate tenderness; movement produces pain. Bowel sounds are absent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management of this patient's hypertension?

choices.B: Increase rate of lactated Ringer solution

correctExplanation: Appropriate pain control is important in preventing postoperative complications. This patient has abdominal pain associated with hypertension, tachycardia, and respiratory splinting (eg, shallow breaths due to pain), the latter of which puts her at increased risk for atelectasis and consequent pneumonia. Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) is a frequently used option for controlling postoperative pain with opioid analgesics, such as morphine, hydromorphone, and fentanyl. Typical PCA set-ups include a basal rate, a bolus dose with a lockout interval, and a total hourly limit. Benefits of PCA use include improved patient satisfaction, titratability, and decreased risk for sedation given the frequent, smaller boluses, as compared to larger bolus doses that would be given less frequently by nursing staff. However, PCAs are associated with an overall increase in opioid usage. Basal rates are rarely used, as they can be associated with increased respiratory depression and overdose; therefore, they are often reserved for opioid tolerant patients. Thus, in this patient with signs of uncontrolled postoperative pain, her bolus of morphine should be increased.

This patient has an appropriate blood pressure, and her tachycardia is more likely secondary to uncontrolled pain, rather than hypovolemia. questionStem: A 67-year-old man comes to the physician for a routine health maintenance examination. He feels well. He has hypertension well controlled with enalapril. Five years ago, he underwent coronary artery bypass grafting. He smoked two packs of cigarettes daily for 20 years but stopped smoking 20 years ago. He walks 1 mile daily. His temperature is 37°C (98.6°F), pulse is 84/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 125/78 mm Hg. Cardiopulmonary examination shows no abnormalities. Abdominal examination shows a nontender pulsatile mass in the mid abdomen; no bruits are heard. Femoral pulses are normal. Abdominal ultrasonography shows a 4-cm aneurysm; there is no evidence of rupture. Which of the following factors provides the best rationale for serial imaging rather than surgical repair in this patient?

choices.C: The patient's history of cardiac disease

correctExplanation: An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) refers to a dilation of the abdominal aorta (> 3 cm), most commonly occurring inferior to the take-off of the renal arteries. questionStem: A 29-year-old man with a 6-year history of end-stage renal disease undergoes uneventful renal transplantation. There is immediate diuresis of the kidney with urine output greater than 500 mL/h. Over the next several days, his serum creatinine concentration decreases to normal, and serum phosphorus concentration decreases to 1.5 mg/dL. The decrease in the serum phosphorus concentration is most likely because of which of the following?
correctExplanation: Chronic kidney disease results in secondary and tertiary hyperparathyroidism caused by derangement of calcium and phosphate homeostasis. As the failing kidney is unable to regulate the level of blood calcium and phosphorus, parathyroid hormone (PTH) concentrations increase to promote increased serum calcium from gut, renal, and bone absorption, and to promote renal excretion of phosphorus. PTH levels remain persistently high in renal failure, and even after transplantation, the increased level can persist for several months or even a year or more. Following renal transplantation, the graft kidney will appropriately respond to PTH, which will result in reabsorption of calcium, and excretion of phosphorus. There are multiple proposed mechanisms beyond PTH to explain post-transplant hypophosphatemia, though PTH is postulated to play a primary role. Post-transplant, the kidney is also able to produce active Vitamin D, a function also lost in end-stage kidney disease. Vitamin D promotes gastrointestinal absorption of calcium and phosphorus, further contributing to restored serum levels of both, and affecting feedback on the parathyroid gland to produce PTH. The mechanism of electrolyte homeostasis following transplant is complex, though PTH and Vitamin D, among several other factors, play key roles.

questionStem: A 37-year-old woman with stage IV breast cancer is admitted to the hospital because of lethargy and right thigh pain for the past 3 days. Her pulse is 100/min, respirations are 10/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mm Hg. Physical examination shows dry mucous membranes. Mental status examination shows deficits in short-term memory. correctExplanation: Hypercalcemic crisis secondary to malignancy-associated hypercalcemia is the most likely cause of the patient’s symptoms. Acute hypercalcemia can present with a broad spectrum of symptoms and can be life-threatening because of its effect on neuronal conduction, the cardiac action potential, kidney function, and volume status. It commonly presents with constipation, lethargy, weakness, and altered mental status. It can result in a short QT interval and nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, leading to significant dehydration. Her temperature is 36.2°C (97.1°F), pulse is 98/min, and blood pressure is 110/70 mm Hg. She is intubated and mechanically ventilated. The family agrees to organ donation but requests proof of brain death other than the physical findings. Which of the following is the most effective test to determine brain death?

correctExplanation: Death is a challenging and common situation that physicians will encounter in practice. Though the exact nature of death remains an ongoing debate, the current generally accepted definitions in the medical field are irreversible cessation of circulatory and pulmonary function or irreversible cessation of all functions of the whole brain, which is referred to as brain death. The American Academy of Neurology (AAN) issues guidelines to aid clinicians, medical systems, and patients’ families in accepting a declaration of brain death. The three primary criteria for adult brain death are: known cause of coma and exclusion of any potentially reversible factors, a neurologic examination that tests for brain stem reflexes and a central response to pain, and an apnea test which assesses whether the brain can drive respiratory functions in response to an increase in CO. If there is any remaining uncertainty, certain ancillary tests may be performed to demonstrate an absence of cerebral blood flow. The gold standard for cerebral blood flow studies is cerebral angiography; transcranial ultrasonography, CT or MR angiography, and radionuclide brain imaging can also be used.

questionStem: An 18-year-old woman with ovarian germ cell cancer comes to the physician with her parents to discuss treatment options. Her condition has progressed despite chemotherapy, and the chemotherapy has caused multiple adverse effects. Her parents have researched a new experimental treatment protocol that would involve bone marrow transplantation but would only have a 5% 2-year survival likelihood. The daughter does not want to undergo transplantation because she says that she is ready to die. Her parents are distraught and want to do everything possible to improve her prognosis. The ethical principle that applies most strongly in this case is autonomy, the right of the patient to ultimately decide what treatments they do and do not receive. In respecting autonomy, it is implied that the patient has capacity to make rational, informed, and voluntary decisions with reason and understanding. Society recognizes that age is a factor in the ability to make a fully reasoned choice with understanding, and the age at which patients are considered to have full autonomy is determined by the legal system. Generally, patients that are 18 years of age or older are considered to have full autonomy in medical decision-making. In this case, the moral decision is to respect the wishes of the patient.
